summary: Top Traders Unplugged Systematic Investor Ep.412 (Aug 2026): Harry Moore (Man Group) and Niels discuss July/August 2026 trend-following dispersion (speed, market universe, yen intervention, AI-trade unwind), AI productivity in quant research, and two papers. Main points: trend is a cash-efficient, left-tail-uncorrelated alpha for portable alpha (needs about 40% cash, rebalancing/swap vs futures choices), and the Turtle rules map to volatility sizing, Kelly and drawdown-control mathematics.

coverage.note: nothing actionable: greetings, books and old phones small talk
Situational Awareness fund blow-up (theme concentration), BOJ/Fed yen intervention
Intervention vs rules-based trend, position sizing, 10-sigma move; trend barometer; July dispersion drivers
Themes (semis/software) dispersion, levered ETF decay, index performance data, CTA positioning, trend speed comparison starts
Speed results (20/60/130/260 day), slow outperformance, market-universe dispersion in energies
Fixed income dispersion, cross-sectional equity sector models, quality factor; AI trade bubble vs upside framing
AI bubble vs upside scenario, productivity gains, illusion of diversification in a 30-40% drawdown
Bonds also selling off, trend as left-tail diversifier, AI generation junior skills
AI changes quant researcher time split, hiring and testing
Humans reviewing code; cash efficiency of trend, freeing cash for cross-sectional/carry alphas
Cash-efficient access when private capital is illiquid; portable alpha construction; stacking returns
Portable alpha paper motivation, 2008 failure causes, cash buffer setup
Margin and cash buffers: 20% vs 40%, Monte Carlo, forced de-risking cost
Operational preference for no margin calls, liquid alpha, rebalancing replicates index issue
Rebalancing rule effects, swaps vs futures, caution on back-tested combinations; Turtle paper introduced
Turtle paper: range volatility estimate, Parkinson, volatility-based position sizing
Kelly criterion, Thorp, 2N stop equals 2% equity, correlation caps
Turtle drawdown rules and Grossman-Zhou, risk management is the edge
Leverage as tool, risk-balance of 50/50, choosing alpha uncorrelated in left tail
Check alpha vs worst 5% beta periods, trend negative correlation, volatility scaling lowers margin; outro

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: even if on paper you look somewhat like dollar neutral or market neutral
claims.claim: A hedge fund that is dollar or market neutral on paper can still be concentrated in one theme (the other side of the AI trade), so a theme reversal caused a large loss; being right does not prevent trouble.
claims.conditions: when a book is built around a single theme despite neutral beta
claims.testable: partly: factor/theme concentration can be measured

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neils")
claims.quote: that diversification uh really does uh u matter
claims.claim: A 45 billion fund losing about two thirds in weeks shows that concentration and leverage on one idea are dangerous and diversification matters.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neils")
claims.quote: intervening uh in the Japanese yen only a couple of days before month end which you know it did have an effect
claims.claim: Joint central-bank intervention in the yen hit trend followers who were short yen, though past interventions did not last long.
claims.direction: yen up, trend short-yen positions hurt
claims.conditions: when intervention follows a long one-way yen move
claims.testable: yes: intervention dates and trend returns are public

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neils")
claims.quote: Humans start to panic. The rulesbased systems don't.
claims.claim: Rules-based systems hold uncomfortable positions through intervention rumours while humans panic and exit.
claims.testable: partly: systematic vs discretionary reaction can be compared

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neils")
claims.quote: it's the importance of stizing and and making sure that that one position um can't can't hit you too much
claims.claim: Position sizing must be set so that a single position (such as the yen) cannot hurt the portfolio too much when an intervention reverses it.
claims.testable: yes: size caps vs loss can be tested

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neils")
claims.quote: I think it was like a 10 standard deviation move
claims.claim: The yen intervention produced a roughly 10 standard deviation move, rare and hard to simulate in market data, though such events exist.
claims.testable: partly: tail events are rare in samples

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: when you've when you've had a move go so far for for so long
claims.claim: Authorities intervene when a move has run so far for so long that natural market forces are not reversing it.
claims.testable: partly: intervention after extremes is testable

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neils")
claims.quote: my trend barometer finished yesterday at 27. And that's a very low reading actually.
claims.claim: A trend barometer reading of 27 is a weak signal, implying a soft start to August for trend followers.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: choices of whether to exclude certain markets or whole asset classes would have created a lot a lot of dispersion in in July
claims.claim: July dispersion among trend managers came from asset-class risk weights, market inclusion choices and model speed, with long oil and long stocks positions diverging in outcome.
claims.testable: yes: dispersion across indices is public

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: if you were trend following themes and you were you were long let's say u tech hardware companies you're long semiconductors and you were um uh short kind of software like that would have would have hurt
claims.claim: Thematic trend positions (long tech hardware/semis, short software) were hurt in July, accounting for dispersion among managers.
claims.testable: partly: theme baskets can be backtested

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neils")
claims.quote: the stock had gone up like 120% and then down to flat for over a 3 months period but the 2x levered uh ETF was down like 40 plus% for that period
claims.claim: A 2x levered ETF lost over 40% while the underlying stock round-tripped to flat, showing volatility decay in levered retail products.
claims.testable: yes: path-dependence of levered ETFs is mathematically testable

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neils")
claims.quote: The sock gen CG index is down 88 basis points up 7.15% so far this year.
claims.claim: Early August 2026 trend index data: SG CTA index about -0.9% for the month, +7.15% YTD, BTOP50 +7.17% YTD, trend index +6.89%, short-term traders +3.3% YTD, MSCI World +12.5% YTD, S&P 500 +12.8% YTD.
claims.indicator: SG CTA, SG Trend, BTOP50, S&P 500

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: CTAs are still long equities probably long metals probably as you said long energies um probably long the dollar I would imagine and then still most likely short fixed income
claims.claim: Estimated CTA positioning in Aug 2026: long equities, metals, energies and dollar; short fixed income.
claims.direction: long equities, metals, energies, dollar; short bonds
claims.testable: partly: replication of positioning from trend signals possible

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: if you had chosen a 20-day look back, again, this is just from this specific model, um, you would actually have been down uh, this year
claims.claim: In 2026 YTD a standard trend model was negative at a 20-day lookback, less negative at 60, slightly positive at 130 and best at 260 days, so slower speeds did better.
claims.conditions: in a year without persistent turning points
claims.testable: yes: speed-sorted trend returns can be computed

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neils")
claims.quote: we haven't had a a a turning point that that's that's persisted for long enough for for for the faster speeds to to kind of shine
claims.claim: Faster trend speeds win only after turning points that persist; absent those, slow models (short bonds, long energy, long stocks held throughout) outperform, echoing recent years.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neils")
claims.quote: my my view is always to have some dynamism there that you can you can still capture some of those turning points
claims.claim: Blend some faster speeds with slow models to capture turning points.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: markets have have just tended to be a little bit more rangebound than we've seen in the more traditional energy markets this year
claims.claim: Alternative markets (Nordic and Italian power) were more rangebound than crude and heating oil in 2026, so market universe drives trend performance dispersion.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: you've got the administrator administration shouting for uh rate cuts rate cuts you have markets follow that occasionally then you look at the inflation you look at rising deficits
claims.claim: Fixed income has been difficult for trend for years because opposing forces (political pressure for rate cuts vs inflation and deficits) produce choppy reversals, more so in smaller markets such as Polish swaps.
claims.conditions: when policy and fundamentals pull in opposite directions
claims.testable: partly: trend returns in bonds are testable

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: These cross-sectional models, I mean, from a from a high level have also been profitable just in a very very different way
claims.claim: Cross-sectional sector and factor trend models (semis vs software, value, momentum, quality) were profitable in 2026 but differently from index trend; quality struggled.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: all of these comparisons back to the railroads back to laying cable in the.com bust
claims.claim: AI is compared to railroads and dotcom cable building as a likely capex bubble.
claims.testable: partly: capex booms and subsequent returns can be studied

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: It's got all the hallmarks of these prior periods where capex went through the roof.
claims.claim: Bear case: AI shares the hallmarks of past bubbles (capex surge, mania) that end badly for markets even if useful infrastructure remains.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: Maybe there is this huge upside scenario where um the trade that we saw go wrong last month is the right trade and it works over over the next 10 years.
claims.claim: Stay balanced: the AI trade could also be right for 10 years, so one cannot predict and portfolios should be built for either outcome.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: Now on paper, you look diversified, right? These assets they seem to have kind of in normal times somewhat low correlations with each other.
claims.claim: A portfolio of equities, bonds, commodities and private assets appears diversified in normal times but may all fall together in a 30-40% S&P crash.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: they may mark down more slowly but at some point you're going to take hits there
claims.claim: Private assets mark down slowly and return capital slowly, so they give only paper protection in a crash.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: Then in bonds and gold like earlier in the year we saw again both of those sell off in a in a fairly correlated manner.
claims.claim: Bonds and gold have sold off together, so they were not a reliable hedge for equity drawdowns in an inflationary environment.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: do they have the tools to really cut rates uh like we've seen in in the past to to kind of boy markets
claims.claim: With inflation above target for many years, the Fed may not be able to cut rates to rescue markets, leaving bonds also vulnerable to a hard sell-off.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: trend doesn't have a long-term view on any of these markets right it trades them all
claims.claim: Trend follows prices across assets, going short bonds and equities or long commodities as narratives change, with no long-term view.
claims.direction: short bonds and equities in inflation shock; long commodities

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: It might even go short the AI theme
claims.claim: Trend following can short equities and even the AI theme (semis and hardware) in a break, offering something different from other holdings.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: typically it's it's trend following that is that is zero or or kind of negatively correlated and other asset classes uh of correlations typically typically pick up
claims.claim: In a left-tail shock, trend following is zero or negatively correlated to equities while other asset class correlations rise, making it a covariance-matrix diversifier.
claims.indicator: trend vs equity correlation in stress
claims.direction: long trend in portfolio for tail protection

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: very very difficult to come up with brand new kind of quantitative high alpha ideas
claims.claim: AI summarises existing knowledge but cannot easily produce new alpha ideas, so it frees researchers to be creative rather than write Python.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: if you could split that 50/50 and make it more like 9010 so that your top researchers have plenty more time to think and be creative
claims.claim: AI shifts quant research time from implementation (Python, backtest setup) toward ideas, from about 50/50 to 90/10, squeezing junior implementation roles.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: give someone an AI generated piece, get them to get them to go and critically analyze it
claims.claim: Test researchers by having them critique an AI-generated piece, since AI use is unavoidable; the risk is skill atrophy from one-click answers.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: if I only need to use $20 or $25 to get my $100 of trend following gives me a few new levers
claims.claim: Trend on futures needs only about $20-25 of capital per $100 exposure, so allocators can add trend without selling existing holdings.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: It had lower correlation. It still had positive sharp. It was still additive
claims.claim: Freed cash can fund extra alphas such as cross-sectional trend or carry, which have lower correlation, positive Sharpe and add value.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: Imagine again, you're not getting your cash flows back as as fast as you want from from your private allocations.
claims.claim: Cash-efficient trend allows an allocation even when private assets are not returning capital quickly.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neils")
claims.quote: actually you get almost the sum of the two return stream
claims.claim: Combining trend and equities in portable alpha yields roughly the sum of both return streams rather than the average.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: how should I rebalance portable alpha or how much cash should I hold in a portable alpha structure like you don't find great answers
claims.claim: Second-order portable-alpha design questions (rebalancing rule, cash buffer) are under-researched, motivating the paper.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: in 2008 many of these structures failed right and the lines down which those structures failed those risks still exist
claims.claim: Portable alpha structures failed in 2008 due to insufficient liquidity and alpha-beta correlation; resilient designs must survive the GFC, the dotcom bust and COVID.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: if you've only supported your S&P with $10 of capital and the S&P falls by 10%. All of your margin is gone, right?
claims.claim: A futures- or swap-based beta needs unencumbered cash beyond margin, because a 10% fall exhausts 10% margin and counterparties call for more.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: you get fully drawn down um in the GFC in the dotcom and in co
claims.claim: A 20% unencumbered cash buffer on S&P plus trend would have been fully drawn down in the GFC, dotcom and COVID, forcing beta sales.
claims.indicator: S&P 500 plus SG Trend backtest 26-27 years

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: if you were were selling in the early part of 2009 at a at a low in your equity component and you're knocked out that position, you miss kind of 29 30% of of upside.
claims.claim: Forced beta selling at the lows loses the rebound (about 30% in 2009) and produces large tracking error against the benchmark.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: about once in every 1 to 200 years
claims.claim: About 40% cash (10% margin plus 30% unencumbered) means a forced degearing only once in 100-200 years, per Monte Carlo and real data.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: you've only had one one path of of the truth that actually happened
claims.claim: Only one historical path exists, so Monte Carlo is used to simulate severe drawdowns beyond the history.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: They do not want to be getting margin calls um on a Monday.
claims.claim: Most investors want the manager to bear operational and cash-flow complexity, so a larger buffer is preferred over callable capital.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: If you if you have something that's like weekly dealing or monthly dealing, you can recapitalize quickly.
claims.claim: Liquid alphas such as trend allow quick recapitalisation, making them good candidates for portable alpha.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: as soon as you select a monthly rebalance, you no longer replicate the S&P.
claims.claim: Rebalancing the beta component periodically causes tracking error versus the index; to track closely, buy and hold or use tolerance bands.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: if my S&P and SG trend goes more than 10% out of whack, I will rebalance.
claims.claim: Recommended compromise: rebalance only when the S&P and trend sleeves drift more than about 10% out of balance.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: Every time you rebalance you reby you increase your equity allocation into a continually falling equity market.
claims.claim: In 2008 rebalancing back to target lost money because equities kept falling while trend rose; only buy and hold did better.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: over the long run, we found that in performance terms it kind of doesn't matter.
claims.claim: Over the long run rebalancing frequency (monthly, quarterly, annual, 5-10% bands) makes little performance difference, but it matters in episodes such as 2008 and COVID.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: if you run this over time, it washes out, right? The you don't get a a a structural performance advantage
claims.claim: Swap financing cost (about 40bp) is implicit in futures, so swaps vs futures give no structural performance advantage; the choice is operational, with futures lacking counterparty risk.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neils")
claims.quote: we have seen uh some other combinations that may look great in a back test
claims.claim: Other popular stacked combinations may look great in backtests but hide risks not exposed in recent decades, partly through correlations.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: rules of thumb hand calculable pen and paper easy to do in a in a few minutes uh approximations of later decision theory mathematics
claims.claim: The Turtle rules were hand-calculable approximations of later decision and probability theory.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: they use a rangebased estimate estimator very simple to update each day
claims.claim: The Turtles estimated volatility N with a range-based exponential estimator (half-life about 14 days), consistent with Parkinson's efficient range estimator.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: really what this is is this is volatility based um position sizing, right?
claims.claim: Turtle units equalise risk across markets (one unit of crude equals one unit of Treasuries in risk), i.e. volatility-based position sizing.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: Now any prudent manager will be on the left side of that hill, right? You are taking a little bit of less of the the upside for a much lower probability of of ruin.
claims.claim: The Turtles' 2% equity per 2N stop corresponds to a fractional-Kelly size on the left of the optimum, giving up some growth for much lower ruin risk.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: this equate this 2n equates to 2% of your total equity in your book
claims.claim: A stop at 2N equals a loss of 2% of equity per position.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: the way they dealt with correlations was not in the actual construction but it was on position size caps.
claims.claim: Turtles managed correlation with position-size caps on correlated markets instead of covariance inversion.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: like you cannot stomach an 80% draw down
claims.claim: Because managers run others' money, drawdown-control rules are needed; the Turtles cut equity 20% after a 10% loss, later formalised by Grossman and Zhou.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: they lost 10% um in the market then they would cut their equity by 20%
claims.claim: Turtle drawdown rule: after losing 10% reduce book equity used for sizing by 20%.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neils")
claims.quote: the genius was not so much in buying a 100 day breakout
claims.claim: The Turtles' edge was risk management and scaling rather than the breakout entry.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neils")
claims.quote: we are probably risk managers first and foremost
claims.claim: Trend followers control risk, not returns: small losses, intelligent scaling and surviving to catch outsized moves.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: 85% of the risk is equities, 15% is bonds, even though on paper it says 50/50
claims.claim: A 50/50 portfolio holds roughly 85% of its risk in equities, so leverage on bonds improves risk balance and Sharpe versus a $100 capital constraint.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: you get a higher sharp um than you would by by by having the $100 constraint
claims.claim: Leverage is a portfolio-construction tool that can raise Sharpe when assets are risk-balanced.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: What you also need to really investigate is not just that it's uncorrelated, but that it's uncorrelated in the left tail.
claims.claim: Choose a portable alpha that is uncorrelated in the left tail; liquidity-provision strategies (short vol, merger arbitrage, basis trade) look good normally but have big left tails.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: like the worst 5% of beta returns, like the worst equity periods, and check that you still have no correlation
claims.claim: Test alpha vs the worst 5% of beta returns; trend historically has low to negative correlation to equities in the worst periods.
claims.indicator: trend vs equity correlation in worst 5%

claims.speaker: Harry Moore (Man Group, systematic/trend researcher)
claims.quote: Trend is actually reducing positions. It needs less margin to ride.
claims.claim: Trend scales positions inversely with volatility, so it needs less margin in turning-point stress, unlike liquidity-provision strategies.
